summary: Explore tender management with expert tips, steps, and best practices. Create compelling proposals, streamline submissions, and boost efficiency with AI tools like Inventive.ai.
body_text: Tender management is the process of actually preparing and submitting a tender in response to a request from a client. Most of the time in the form of an RFP. It involves everything from the tender document collection to writing a captivating proposal and ensuring all deadlines are adhered to. The Tender Process Explained The tender process usually starts when there is a need for a particular company to procure goods or services. The company will write an inquiry letter to request suppliers or contractors in the market space to send them a tender. So that they can fulfill the needs of the client and then cost it to them. Tender management in today's fast-moving technologically advanced world is especially interested in emerging technologies. Current trends in Government RFPs, especially for GWACs and IDIQ contracts, emphasize on experience with leading-edge technologies. This requirement underlines the realization by the government that technology plays a very significant role in response and recovery during crises. In fact, companies should have the ability for quick adaptation, innovation, and delivery of solutions in high-stakes environments. This translates to ability in innovations such as 5G, Artificial Intelligence, Augmented Reality, Blockchain, and Cybersecurity, among others. Effective tender management will not only require a documentation of projects executed in the past but also involvement in current research and development. Tender Management for Government Contracts and the Role of GovTech Managing tenders for government contracts can be really cumbersome. Unlike private tenders, the government contracts entail a number of rules and regulations in order to make everything fair, transparent, and accountable. Which, to some extent, may seem overwhelming to the business entering into this area for the first time. However, govTech companies do their part in making these processes easy for businesses to pursue government procurement. Here's how GovTech is helping: Process Automation: GovTech platforms, like Inventive.AI , automate document submission, compliance checks, and communication in the RFP process. This makes the process faster and reduces manual workload, thereby enabling government agencies to become more efficient and fair with respect to their procurement practices. Improved Accessibility: Technologies make it easy for smaller businesses to participate in government tenders. For instance, platforms have tools designed to help easily create and submit RFPs while ensuring compliance and document quality. Enhanced transparency: Periscope Holdings is a veteran govTech space that offers solutions to manage the full RFP cycle. Their systems manage procurement electronically for public agencies from posting prices to awarding contracts. Activities are, therefore, traceable and transparent, building trust among vendors and governmental entities. Tender Management for Government Contracts and the Role of GovTech Tender management for government contracts can become complex. When compared to private tenders, government contracts are pegged to a great deal of rules and regulations that ensure fairness, transparency, and accountability in the process. In fact, this makes it overwhelming, especially when companies are new to dealing with the government. However, govTech companies bridge the gap in these processes, making it quite easy for companies to understand the complexities of government procurement. For example, Inventive.ai is an innovative online platform that uses artificial intelligence to automate the RFP process. Simply put, through the assistance of the inventive.ai platform, public agencies, and vendors can create, organize, and respond to RFPs efficiently, saving time and effort. The AI capabilities of the platform drive consistency, accuracy, and personalization of responses per specific requirements. It makes management from the tender side of government much easier. Such automation saves not only time but also enhances the quality and compliance of the submissions. Thus, making businesses of all scales more effective participants of government contracts. Let us broadly define the most important steps in the tender process: Credits: What Is the Procurement Life Cycle? 16 Stages Explained | NetSuite Why is Tender Management Important? Effective tender management becomes key to directly benefit a company's potential in acquiring new contracts. Thus, growing the business. Proper administration of the tender management process may result in winning the bid while the company loses opportunities and valuable resources otherwise. Key Benefits of Effective Tender Management: Increased Success Rate: A methodical approach toward tender management helps in making a highly competitive, strong, and compliant bid. Better Resource Allocation: With a structured approach, companies can optimize resources better and prevent the wastage of worthwhile time and money on bids that are likely to not be won. Risk Mitigation: Proper tender management enables companies to identify any potential risks at the earlier stages of the process so that they can work to mitigate the risks before they become major issues. Better Client Relationships: A professional and well-organized tender can speak well of the company and reflect positively on the client, potentially bettering future business relationships. Ideas for Improving Your Tender Management Tender processes can be hard, from the point of view of the responder. By using some of the best practices, standing a better chance of winning those tough tenders. Tender processes can be daunting for businesses looking to win lucrative contracts. From navigating complex requirements to facing fierce competition, responding to Requests for Proposals (RFPs) is no easy feat. However, by implementing proven best practices in tender management, RFP responders can significantly improve their chances of success. 1. Completely Understand the RFP : Every tender management process must begin with an understanding of the RFP. It's the document that gives all the pertinent details about client needs, project scope, and evaluation criteria. Spend time going through the RFP to ensure you understand it properly. Tip: List key requirements and evaluation criteria in the RFP. Use these as a checklist which your services are to satisfy. Also you can check all about RFPs from our previous blogs. 2. Do a Feasibility Study : You need to do a feasibility study pertaining to your company and capability vis-à-vis the customers' requirements. There is a need to undertake a feasibility study regarding the company's technical ability, availability of resources, and its financial capability to undertake the project. Tip: To be frank concerning the capabilities and weaknesses of your company. If the project scope is not within your current capability, very likely it's better for you to stay away from it; tendering for a weak reason is not in anyone's interest. 3. Develop a Project Plan : A good tender must have a project plan laid out very well, indicating how you will deliver the project, by when, and what key deliverables or outcomes are expected at major project delivery milestones. This should also cover any foreseen difficulties and possible ways of dealing with them. Tip: Having a proper timeline in the project plan, ensure it is broken down to show the deliverable in phases. This gives the client the impression that, with a properly paved path, the project can easily meet the deadline. 4. Concentrate on Compliance : One of the main reasons an RFP does not work to drive success is noncompliance by your tender to the criteria set out in the RFP. To overcome this minor point, you must ensure that your tender communicates all criteria of the client in the RFP and addresses any specific instructions in the RFP. Tip: Use a compliance matrix to cross-reference how well your proposal responds to specific RFP requirements. It will help you ensure nothing of importance is left out. 5. Highlight Your Unique Value Proposition : The most important point here is, of course, to find a way of saying how your company stands out from the other bidders in the competitive tendering environment. Stress what is different about your company: expertise, an innovative approach, or cost-effectiveness. Tip: State your proposition with utmost clarity in your executive summary to the tender. This is usually the thing the client reads first; therefore, it has to be an eye-opener. 6. Competitive Financial Proposal : Your financial proposal must be competitive, transparent, and realistic. It should detail clear costs, which could include any contingencies. Underbidding or overbidding on your proposal are going to be huge red flags for the client. Tip: Do a detailed cost-benefit analysis to help the client understand that your proposal provides the best value for money. 7. Review and Revise : After you are completely satisfied that there are neither errors nor omissions, you should also verify the tenders and do so on time. In many cases, you may need to have the tender reviewed by somebody not directly involved in the preparation to give a fresh, clear perspective. Checklist: Make sure that there are no important documents missing. Your tender should be formatted according to the client's requirements. 8. Submit on Time : Make the deadline an absolute criteria. Late submissions and some other ones are usually disqualified, even if the tender is the strongest. Make sure to allow plenty of time for the unexpected delays, such as technical problems, or courier problems. Hint: Try to put in your tender at least the day before the deadline, to eliminate the hassle of any last-minute problems. Tender management is a complex process that is key to any business exploring new contracts as a way of expanding. A step-by-step approach with a focus in areas such as compliance, project planning, and added value would give you better chances and possibilities of success. Understanding and mastering the management process for tenders from the RFP responder's perspective is how one obtains more wins and the ability to grow their business more effectively. With the correct strategy, tender management can be converted into an effective tool to grow and succeed in business. Ready to Streamline your Tender Management process? title: What Are the Best Alternatives to a Grass Lawn?
summary: If you want to replace a traditional grass lawn, some of the best alternatives include native plants, drought-tolerant landscaping, ground covers, wildflower or meadow gardens, hardscaping, decorative gravel, artificial turf, rain gardens, and raised garden beds. The right lawn alternative depends on your climate, rainfall, sunlight, foot traffic, maintenance preferences, and how you want to [...]
body_text: If you want to replace a traditional grass lawn, some of the best alternatives include native plants, drought-tolerant landscaping, ground covers, wildflower or meadow gardens, hardscaping, decorative gravel, artificial turf, rain gardens, and raised garden beds. The right lawn alternative depends on your climate, rainfall, sunlight, foot traffic, maintenance preferences, and how you want to use your outdoor space. Replacing all or part of a lawn can reduce mowing and, depending on the landscaping you choose, may also reduce watering and other maintenance. Here are several grass alternatives to consider for your yard. 1. Xeriscaping for a Lower-Water Yard Xeriscaping is a landscaping approach designed to reduce or eliminate the need for supplemental irrigation. It typically combines water-efficient plants with thoughtful soil preparation, mulch, efficient irrigation when needed, and landscaping materials such as gravel or stone. Although xeriscaping is often associated with dry climates, its water-conscious principles can be adapted to many regions. Choosing native or climate-appropriate plants is key to creating a landscape suited to local conditions. 2. Ground Covers as Grass Alternatives If you want to keep some greenery without maintaining a traditional turfgrass lawn, certain ground covers may be an option. Depending on your climate and growing conditions, alternatives can include clover, creeping thyme, moss, and other low-growing plants. Some can tolerate light foot traffic, but suitability varies considerably by species, sunlight, soil, moisture, and region. Before replacing a lawn with ground cover, check with a local nursery or extension service to determine which plants are appropriate for your area. 3. Native Grasses and Wildflower Gardens Native grasses and wildflowers can replace portions of a traditional lawn with a more natural landscape. Once established, plants adapted to local conditions may require less supplemental water and maintenance than conventional turfgrass. Native plantings can also provide food and habitat for pollinators and other wildlife. Look for plants or seed mixes specifically recommended for your region, and check that the species are appropriate and noninvasive where you live. 4. Hardscaping for Outdoor Living Space If you would rather use part of your lawn for entertaining or relaxing, consider replacing grass with hardscaping. Common hardscape options include: Pavers or brick for patios and walkways Concrete for patios, seating areas, and paths Wood decking for elevated outdoor living areas Composite decking for a lower-maintenance alternative to traditional wood Gravel or stone for paths, seating areas, and landscaping Hardscaping can turn unused lawn into space for outdoor dining, seating, grilling, or entertaining while reducing the amount of grass you need to mow. 5. Gravel, Stone, and Other Low-Maintenance Materials Decorative gravel, pebbles, river rock, and other landscaping stone can replace grass in areas where greenery isn’t necessary. These materials can work particularly well for pathways, borders, seating areas, and water-wise landscapes. However, consider drainage, heat, weeds, and local climate before covering a large area with stone. Artificial turf is another grass alternative that doesn’t require mowing or irrigation for growth. It may be useful in certain high-traffic areas, but homeowners should consider factors such as surface temperature, drainage, installation costs, and long-term maintenance before choosing it. 6. Rain Gardens for Areas That Collect Water If part of your yard regularly collects stormwater runoff, a rain garden may be a useful alternative to turfgrass. Rain gardens are shallow planted areas designed to temporarily collect and absorb runoff. They typically use plants suited to both wet and dry conditions. The appropriate location, size, and plants depend on your property’s drainage patterns, soil, and local climate. 7. Raised Garden Beds for a Productive Yard Replacing part of your lawn with raised garden beds can turn unused grass into space for growing vegetables, herbs, fruits, or flowers. Raised beds still require watering and regular upkeep, so they aren’t necessarily a low-maintenance lawn alternative. However, they can make your outdoor space more productive and give you something in return for the time you spend maintaining it. Should You Replace Your Entire Lawn? You don’t have to remove your entire lawn at once. Replacing one section at a time can make the project more manageable and help you determine which landscaping options work best for your property. You might start by turning one section into a native plant garden, adding a small patio, installing raised beds, or replacing turf in a difficult-to-mow area. Before making major changes, check local landscaping regulations, HOA requirements, and any restrictions that may apply. How to Choose the Best Lawn Alternative The best grass alternative depends on what you want your yard to do. Consider: Water use: Native plants and xeriscaping may help reduce supplemental irrigation. Maintenance: Hardscaping and some ground covers can reduce mowing, although every option requires some upkeep. Foot traffic: Patios, pathways, and other durable surfaces may work better in frequently used areas. Wildlife: Native grasses, flowers, and other native plants can provide habitat and food sources. Food production: Raised beds can turn lawn space into a vegetable or herb garden. Drainage: Rain gardens may help manage runoff in appropriately located areas. Climate: Choose plants and materials suited to your region’s temperature, rainfall, soil, and sunlight. Make Room While You Redesign Your Yard A lawn replacement project can temporarily leave you with extra garden tools, patio furniture, outdoor equipment, planters, and other seasonal items competing for space. If you need more room while redesigning your yard, Public Storage offers storage units in a range of sizes for household and outdoor items. Moving items you’re not currently using into self storage can help clear your garage, shed, or work area while you tackle the project. Find a Public Storage location near you to compare available unit sizes and storage features.

title: HungerRush POS Review: What Operators Should Know About the Pizza-First System
summary: HungerRush starts at $199 a month and owns pizza menus. A full POS review, then its OrderAI phone agent compared with Certus AI on menu truth and payment.
body_text: Key takeaways HungerRush is a cloud POS built for pizza, quick service, and delivery-heavy operations. More than 18,000 restaurants run it, including Hungry Howie's and Jet's Pizza locations. The reason to pick it is the menu engine: half-and-half toppings, quarters, slices, and size-based pricing that generalist systems handle with workarounds. Pricing starts at $199 a month before hardware, processing, and add-ons, which lands above most of the mainstream category. This review is in two parts: the POS on its own merits, then OrderAI, its phone AI, compared straight with Certus. Pizza is still a phone business - 39% of pizza customers order by phone call, more than any other channel. At Certus we work with hundreds of restaurants across every major POS, and phone AI is our whole business, so read this knowing where I stand. This review runs in two parts. Part one is the POS, judged on its own. Part two is the phone: HungerRush's OrderAI next to our Certus, compared straight. I will keep the facts and my opinions clearly separated in both. Part one: the POS What HungerRush is HungerRush, formerly known as Revention, is a cloud-based restaurant POS aimed squarely at pizza, quick service, and delivery operations. More than 18,000 restaurants use it, and the marquee names are pizza chains: Hungry Howie's and Jet's Pizza among them. This is not a general-purpose till stretched to fit pizza. It is a pizza system first, and reviewers score it well for exactly that fit. The pizza test: why not just use Clover? Here is the question that actually decides this purchase. Any modern POS can ring up a pepperoni pie. The test is Friday night's real orders: half pepperoni, half mushroom, extra cheese on one half only. A large that costs $2 more than the medium, but $3 more with stuffed crust. Slices at lunch, whole pies at dinner, quarters for the family deal. A generalist like Clover or Square can be configured to handle most of this, but you are bending the system: modifiers stacked on modifiers, and your staff pay for it in taps and workarounds during the rush. I have reviewed both, and they are excellent systems for the restaurants they were built for. Pizza is not that restaurant. HungerRush builds its menu structure around exactly these orders. That is the single strongest reason it wins pizza shops. If your menu lives on customization - toppings by the half and quarter, size-dependent pricing, slice sales - the menu engine is the difference between a 40-second order and a 3-minute one, hundreds of times a week. What the platform covers HungerRush sells itself as one system for the whole operation, and the platform covers a lot: Online ordering from the POS vendor itself, so web orders land in the same queue as everything else. Delivery management with driver tracking and dispatch, the logistics layer most mainstream POS systems leave to third parties. Loyalty and marketing built in, aimed at the repeat-order economics of pizza. Reporting across locations, which matters once you run more than one shop. For a delivery-first operation, that bundle is the pitch: one vendor owns the till, the website, the drivers, and the phone. HungerRush pricing: what you will pay Published pricing starts at $199 a month. That is the entry point, and it sits noticeably above the mainstream category, where software tiers start at $0 to $69 at Toast and $29.99 at SkyTab . Independent review sites make the same point: itqlick's expert review scores HungerRush 7.5 out of 10 and calls it excellent for pizza and delivery but pricey against competitors. As with every POS I have reviewed, the sticker is the start of the math. Hardware, payment processing, and module add-ons land on top, and quotes are custom. Pin the full number down in writing, ask specifically what OrderAI costs on top of the base system, and check the support terms while you are at it, because user reviews on support responsiveness are mixed. Where it struggles Price is the first flag. The $199 floor lands before hardware, processing, and add-ons, and itqlick's verdict of excellent but pricey matches what custom quotes tend to look like in practice. Support is the second. User reviews on responsiveness are mixed, which weighs heavily in a business where the till going down at 7pm on a Friday is an emergency, not a ticket. The third is the shape of the platform itself. Everything is built for everything else, which is efficient right up until you want to take one piece somewhere else. Nothing in the stack, OrderAI included, comes with you to another POS. All-in-one platforms work this way, and it is fair design. Just price the exit before you sign. The POS verdict If you run a pizza or delivery-first shop with real customization, HungerRush belongs at the top of your shortlist, ahead of the generalists. You are buying the menu engine and the delivery logistics, and both are genuinely built for you. If you are rate-sensitive, get the full quote in writing before you commit, because the gap between $199 and the real monthly number is where this decision gets made. And if you run counter service without delivery, start with the mainstream reviews linked above instead. Part two: the phone If pizza is your business, the phone is too Pizza is still a phone business. CivicScience survey data from February 2026 shows more pizza customers order by phone call, 39%, than any other channel, ahead of the restaurant's own website at 34%. If you run the kind of shop HungerRush is built for, your phone rings all night, and you will end up evaluating a voice AI whether you planned to or not. If you land on HungerRush, you have two real options: OrderAI, the phone AI that comes from your POS vendor, or Certus, which is purpose-built for restaurant phones. Here is that comparison, played straight. What OrderAI is OrderAI is HungerRush's own ordering AI, and it comes in two flavors: Talk, which answers phone calls, and Text, which handles orders by SMS. The numbers are real. HungerRush's own page counts more than 10 million AI orders, and Jet's Pizza runs it across more than 350 locations with a 92% order success rate, meaning the AI completes roughly 9 in 10 orders it starts without a human stepping in. Unlimited simultaneous calls means the Friday rush cannot bury it. Credit where due: HungerRush understood before most of the industry that the phone is a revenue channel, and built for it. If you are already on their POS, OrderAI is the default choice, and a reasonable one. It comes from your vendor, on one support line, built for your till. So the fair question is what to compare before you sign. Two things. The first thing: menu truth Every voice AI sounds perfect in a demo, because demos use easy orders. The expensive failure is quieter: the AI agrees to things that do not exist. A half-and-half with a topping you dropped last month. A large at a price from two menus ago. The industry politely calls this hallucination. Your kitchen calls it a refund, a remake, and a one-star review, and on an allergen question it is far worse than that. We built Certus so that mistake cannot happen. The agent is locked to the live menu in your POS. Every item, size, modifier, and price is validated against your till before the ticket fires. If it is not on your menu, Certus cannot sell it, no matter how nicely the caller asks. OrderAI integrates with the full HungerRush menu, which is a real start. What its pages do not publish is the validation mechanism. So ask the question I would put to any voice AI vendor, us included: what stops the agent from selling something I do not serve, and what does it do when a caller asks an allergen question the menu data cannot answer? Listen for a specific answer. The second thing: where payment happens A delivery order is not real until it is paid. HungerRush's own OrderAI page says checkout runs through secure mobile payments via a texted link. A texted link assumes a smartphone in the caller's hand and a caller willing to finish the job after the call ends. The regular ordering from a landline cannot click one at all. Certus takes payment on the call itself, or by link, or at pickup, your choice per order type. An order paid on the call gets made, collected, and never ghosted. For a delivery-heavy shop, that difference compounds every single night. Side by side: OrderAI vs Certus AI OrderAI Certus AI Works with HungerRush POS only All major POS systems including Toast, Square, Clover, Skytab, and Aloha NCR Phone orders Yes - Talk for calls, Text for SMS Yes - full orders with upsells, straight into the POS Payment Texted payment link (per HungerRush's page) On the call, by link, or at pickup - your choice per order type Menu accuracy Full HungerRush menu integration; validation method not published - ask Locked to the live POS menu; every item, size, modifier, and price validated before the ticket fires Spanish Not published - ask Included with English, automatic detection Pricing Not published - custom quote on top of the POS Flat monthly pricing Contract Quoted with the platform - ask 30-day rolling, 30-day money-back guarantee Setup Through HungerRush onboarding Same day Support HungerRush platform support (reviews mixed) Co-founder and engineering direct access One more honest note: if you are not on HungerRush, OrderAI is not on your menu at all. It exists to feed HungerRush tills. Do not switch an entire POS to fix the phone - that is surgery for a problem with an outpatient answer. The verdict On the POS: pizza and delivery-first shops with heavy customization should shortlist HungerRush first, get the full quote in writing, and weigh the mixed support reviews against the strength of the menu engine. On the phone: if you run HungerRush, put OrderAI and Certus through the same two tests, menu truth and payment, and buy whichever passes both for your shop. If you run anything else, OrderAI is not an option, and Certus was purpose-built for the job on the till you already own. Baci Trattoria, a pizza restaurant running on SkyTab , recovered $50,000 in missed-call revenue across more than 1,000 orders by pairing its existing POS with Certus, on flat monthly pricing with a 30-day rolling contract, same-day setup, and a 30-day money-back guarantee. Our Trustpilot rating is 4.5 stars. Book a demo and hear it take a real pizza order, half-and-half toppings included. About the author I'm Gurveer Singh, CEO and co-founder of Certus AI. We work with hundreds of restaurants across every major POS, from single-location independents to chains and franchises. I managed 11 of my family's restaurants by age 17, most of them the kind where Friday night meant a phone ringing off the wall, which is why I ended up building the thing that answers it. And all of it becomes your responsibility the moment it ships. None of this is news to us. Securing the software supply chain is the problem we’re here to solve, and our commitment to it is absolute. The latest round of updates widens the trusted foundation Docker is building under your supply chain, and tightens how it’s enforced. More of the software inside your images is now built and patched by Docker itself. Security coverage continues after software reaches end of life. Images get tailored to your environment without losing their guarantees. And policy enforcement now reaches every developer machine. The details are below. First, where all of this is headed. A trusted foundation for the whole supply chain It all starts from one principle, and Docker Hardened Images was built on it. Security that doesn’t get adopted doesn’t secure anything. The entire catalog is free for every developer, because a secure baseline shouldn’t be a premium feature. Every image is compatible with Alpine and Debian, the distributions your teams already run, and Docker builds every one of them itself, from source. Adoption is a FROM-line change, not a migration project. And every image is independently verifiable, with signed SBOMs (software bills of materials) and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so your auditors work from evidence instead of vendor claims. A year in, the numbers make the case . The catalog has grown past 4,000 hardened images, plus MCP servers, Helm charts, and ELS images. It draws more than 3.5 million pulls a week, with over a million builds running regularly to keep all of it patched, and open source projects like n8n run production on DHI . The catalog grows the way it always has, driven by what customers request. But the goal was never just a catalog. The goal is one trusted foundation under your whole software supply chain, where the images you run, the packages inside them, the charts that deploy them, and the tools your agents call all carry the same provenance. Security becomes the default from day one, and it holds, without asking your teams to change how they work. Docker is leading that charge. Here’s what that looks like in practice. Built from source, down to every package The hardening keeps reaching deeper into the stack. Docker Hardened System Packages take hardening below the image, to the packages inside it, across both Alpine and Debian, with every package built from upstream source, patched, and maintained by Docker in the same SLSA Build Level 3 pipeline that builds the images themselves. And the repository behind them is open to more than the catalog. DHI Enterprise customers can point apt or apk directly at Docker’s hardened package repository and bring the same packages into images they build themselves, extending the hardened supply chain beyond the images Docker ships to every image your organization builds. The coverage keeps widening. What began with Alpine now spans Debian, with Python, the catalog’s most pulled image, among the first to ship fully hardened. The work compounds every week, and the Debian and Alpine package lists are public, so you can watch the catalog harden in real time. If you’ve spent time chasing base-image CVEs, you know why this matters. System packages are notorious for slow fixes; a patch can sit waiting on the distribution’s next release for months or years. Docker doesn’t wait. We patch at the package level, ahead of upstream when it counts, and the fix lands in every image that uses that package, in one build wave instead of image by image. Entire businesses have been built on delivering community-distribution security updates faster than the community. With DHI, that speed is included. The guarantees hold up under inspection, too. Packages you add through DHI customization, tailoring an image to your workloads, come from that same hardened repository, not an unverified public mirror, so they are hardened system packages in their own right and the SLA that covers the base image extends through everything you add. And because one vendor stands behind the image, the packages inside it, the CVE investigation, and the patch, your auditors get a single chain of signed provenance instead of a stack of vendor assurances. Your distribution, meanwhile, stays your distribution. Building a hardened package ecosystem from source is a serious engineering commitment, and Docker made it twice, for Alpine and for Debian, so keeping your house standard never costs you your security posture. Patch past end of life Production software has a habit of outliving its maintainers. Migrations wait on budgets, dependencies, and test cycles, and CVEs don’t wait with them. That’s the problem DHI Extended Lifecycle Support (ELS) exists for. It keeps end-of-life software patched, with SBOMs and provenance maintained, for up to five more years. ELS isn’t limited to a set catalog, either. Docker watches the end-of-life calendar and builds coverage ahead of it, and anything you don’t see, you can request. MinIO is the newest addition. Upstream archived the project in February 2026, yet in the DHI catalog it lives on, patched and hardened, and your migration runs on your schedule instead of upstream’s. Customize at scale, manage as code Nobody runs stock images in production. You add CA certificates, agents, and the packages your applications demand. The trouble is that in most of this market, the first change you make is where the vendor’s guarantees end, and everything after it is yours to carry. DHI customization works the other way around. You define what your images need, and Docker manages the full lifecycle of your customized images, rebuilding them through the same hardened pipeline on every upstream patch. The SBOM, the attestations, and the SLA travel with the customization instead of dying at it. Customization operates at scale, too. Bulk customizations run through the UI, CLI, and API, with YAML configuration and GitHub Actions support, so you can tailor hundreds of repositories in one pass and let the rebuilds take care of themselves. And if your platform runs on Terraform, customization is code as well. The DHI Terraform provider mirrors and customizes hardened images with the same pull requests and reviews as the rest of your infrastructure. The savings are real infrastructure, not a rounding error. Customers tell us they’ve shut off the CI pipelines that existed only to rebuild images, because Docker rebuilds for them. The blind redeploy cadence goes with those pipelines. You ship an update when a fix actually needs to go out, knowing exactly what changed, instead of rebuilding everything on a schedule and hoping QA catches what moved. For organizations whose data-residency requirements keep images inside the EU, EU-hosted customizations arrive in September. Your customized images will live in Docker Hub’s EU region with the same SBOMs, attestations, and SLA as everywhere else. Residency stops being the reason your hardening program waits. Harden beyond base images The same standard keeps moving up the stack. The catalog now carries fully supported Helm charts, so your Kubernetes deployments start hardened too. And it carries a growing set of hardened MCP servers, because the tools your agents call deserve the same scrutiny as the images they run on. Govern it all with Docker Scout policy Scanning tells you what’s wrong. Policy is how you keep it from shipping. And enforcement is where most supply-chain programs quietly fail, because hardened artifacts only protect you when your teams actually use them. Developers move fast and default to what works, and the developer machine is exactly where the current wave of attacks aims. Docker Scout policy closes that gap. It evaluates flexible, customizable policies from the CLI and inside CI, and it ships with the same policies Docker uses to verify every hardened image in the catalog. The policies are written in Rego, the industry standard, and they’re portable, so the same rules that gate a build in your CI travel with your teams to every developer machine in your organization. Gating at the registry matters, but it stops at the registry; developers can route around it all day. Policy that travels to the machine is how you hold every image you run, and every image your teams build, to the bar Docker holds itself to. It’s an additive control. It works alongside the scanners you already run, and it’s already in the Docker subscription you have. The foundation is already in your stack The supply-chain problem is not going to shrink. More code is coming, agents are becoming contributors, and the patch windows regulators expect keep getting shorter. Point tools won’t carry that weight. A foundation that’s secure by default will, backed by an ecosystem that keeps it that way. That is exactly what Docker’s security portfolio delivers. Hardened content on the distributions you already run, customization that keeps its guarantees, support that outlasts upstream, and policy you control, from one vendor accountable for all of it. And none of it asks you to adopt something new. It’s all in the Docker you already run. Your builds, tools, and pipelines stay the same. Your CVE count doesn’t. Browse the DHI catalog and pull your first hardened image today. title: How to Fix MXF Interoperability Issues in Avid, Premiere, Resolve
summary: Learn how to diagnose MXF failures across Avid, Premiere, and Resolve, including audio mismatches, lost metadata, codec conflicts, FFprobe checks, rewraps, and transcodes.
body_text: If an MXF works in one app and fails in another, don't start by transcoding it, but start by identifying which part of the file is incompatible: the wrapper, the codec, the audio layout, or the metadata the next system needs for relink and conform. MXF isn't one format in the way people often talk about it. It's a container, and inside it can be DNxHD, DNxHR, XAVC, AVC-Intra, XDCAM, JPEG 2000, PCM audio, multichannel audio, timecode tracks, reel metadata, camera metadata, and vendor-specific descriptors. Avid, Premiere Pro, and DaVinci Resolve can all work with MXF, but they don't make the same assumptions about every MXF. An MXF wrapper can carry separate video, audio, timecode, and metadata pieces. The practical rule is simple: If the file opens but relink fails, suspect metadata. If picture opens but audio is wrong, suspect channel layout or track mapping. If one app imports and another refuses, suspect codec support, MXF operational pattern, or version-specific decode support. If Avid is involved, be especially careful about OP-Atom versus OP1a and whether you're linking, importing, consolidating, or using managed media. If Premiere is involved, confirm whether the issue is import, relink, interpretation, proxy reconnect, or export settings. That framing saves time because the fix for each problem is different, and rewrapping can solve a wrapper problem without touching the media essence. Re-encoding can solve a codec problem but creates new files, new QC obligations, and possible conform risk. Your team may need to repair metadata with a controlled transcode through a post tool, not a generic command-line conversion. Symptom Likely failing layer First diagnostic move Least destructive fix File opens in one app but is refused by another Wrapper, codec support, or application version Compare format_name , codec_name , profile , and the receiving app's supported formats Update the app or plug-in, change the import or link method, or rewrap if the codec is already supported Picture plays but audio is missing, split, or mapped incorrectly Audio stream layout or channel interpretation Use FFprobe to see whether audio is one multichannel stream or separate mono streams Remap or reinterpret audio in the NLE, or create a controlled audio transcode if the layout must change Media imports but relink, AAF, XML, or conform fails Metadata used for identification Compare source timecode , duration, clip name, reel, tape, and camera roll values Relink with the correct metadata rules, or regenerate media while preserving conform identifiers Avid links the file but will not treat it like managed media OP1a versus OP-Atom workflow, Avid media database expectations, or incomplete descriptors Confirm whether the file is linked through AMA or UME, imported, transcoded, consolidated, or placed in Avid MediaFiles Generate Avid-compatible media through Media Composer, Resolve, or a tested dailies system A desktop player works but an NLE fails Professional codec, metadata, or workflow compatibility Test in the target NLE and compare the FFprobe report against known good files Do not use player playback as QC, test the actual workflow step that fails Why MXF breaks between Avid, Premiere, and Resolve Most MXF failures aren't random because they come from a mismatch between how the file was created and how the receiving application expects to use it. Avid Media Composer has a long history with MXF OP-Atom media inside the Avid MediaFiles/MXF folder structure. Avid also supports linking to generic MXF through AMA, including OP1a-style files, but linked media and managed Avid media aren't the same workflow. Avid documentation is very clear that some operations have limitations with AMA clips , and that you shouldn't mix AMA and traditional import workflows casually. Dynamic Relink and some multicam workflows can behave differently depending on how media entered the project. Premiere Pro is usually more permissive on import, but that doesn't mean it interprets every file the way Avid did. A common surprise is an Avid-originated multichannel audio MXF that appears as multiple mono items or separate audio clips in Premiere. The media may be technically valid, but Premiere’s interpretation doesn't match the expected audio layout. Resolve sits somewhere between the two, and it supports DNxHD and DNxHR workflows used with Avid and can read many MXF variants. But support is still specific to codec, wrapper, bit depth, chroma sampling, operating system, and Resolve version. A Resolve 20 or 21 workstation may accept a file that an older Resolve 17 workstation doesn't. The same .mxf extension tells you almost nothing, so you need to inspect the file. Separate wrapper problems from codec problems The first useful split is wrapper versus codec. The wrapper is the MXF structure: OP1a, OP-Atom, partitioning, timecode tracks, descriptors, and how streams are arranged. The codec is the compressed or uncompressed media essence inside: DNxHD, DNxHR, XAVC-I, XAVC-L, AVC-Intra, XDCAM HD, PCM audio, and so on. These common symptoms point in different directions: File imports in Premiere but not Avid: often wrapper expectations, Avid AMA support, missing plug-ins, or unsupported metadata descriptors . File links in Avid but won't fast import or consolidate as expected: often native versus non-native codec handling, or a difference between linking and managed Avid media. File opens in Resolve but AAF relink fails: often source timecode, reel name, tape name, or clip name mismatch. File plays video but not audio in a desktop player: often not an editing problem at all, since many consumer players don't handle professional MXF audio layouts well. File plays in VLC but fails in an NLE: usually a professional metadata, codec licensing, or workflow compatibility issue rather than basic file corruption. You can sometimes solve a wrapper problem with a rewrap, but you can't solve a codec problem that way. If the receiving system can't decode the essence, copying it into a different container won't help. Use FFprobe to see what you actually have FFprobe is useful because it gives you a neutral view of the container, streams, codecs, timecode, audio layout, and metadata tags. It won't tell you every application-specific behavior, but it will stop the guessing. Inspection tools reveal the streams, layout, and metadata hidden inside a media file. Start with a readable stream summary: ffprobe -hide_banner -i input.mxf For handoff diagnostics, JSON output is easier to save and compare: ffprobe -hide_banner -v error \ -show_format \ -show_streams \ -print_format json \ input.mxf > input.ffprobe.json For a faster look at just stream essentials: ffprobe -hide_banner -v error \ -select_streams v:0 \ -show_entries stream=index,codec_name,codec_long_name,profile,width,height,r_frame_rate,avg_frame_rate,pix_fmt,field_order,time_base,duration_tags:stream_tags=timecode,reel_name,tape \ -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 \ input.mxf For audio layout: ffprobe -hide_banner -v error \ -select_streams a \ -show_entries stream=index,codec_name,channels,channel_layout,sample_rate,bits_per_sample:stream_tags=title,language \ -of table \ input.mxf The useful fields to compare are: format_name , which may show MXF variants recognized by FFmpeg. codec_name and profile , especially for DNxHD, DNxHR, XAVC, AVC-Intra, and PCM audio. width , height , pix_fmt , and field_order . r_frame_rate , avg_frame_rate , and time base. stream count, especially whether audio is one 8-channel stream or eight mono streams. timecode , reel_name , tape , material_package_name , or similar tags. duration differences between audio and video streams. FFprobe isn't the final authority, but you need a file report before deciding whether to relink, reinterpret, rewrap, or re-encode. Avid-specific failure patterns Avid is often where MXF interoperability gets strictest because Avid workflows depend heavily on media management and metadata. There are two very different ways an MXF can appear in Media Composer: Linked media through AMA or UME. Managed media inside the Avid MediaFiles folder structure. Those workflows aren't interchangeable because an MXF OP1a file that links through AMA isn't automatically the same as Avid-native OP-Atom media dropped into Avid MediaFiles/MXF/1 . Avid’s supported formats documentation distinguishes native formats, which Avid can rewrap or fast import, from non-native formats, which require transcoding, and the app may be able to see the file, but that doesn't guarantee it can treat it as native managed media. Common Avid issues include: OP1a files link but don't behave like Avid managed media. OP-Atom files created outside Avid are missing metadata Avid expects. DNxHD or DNxHR essence is valid, but the MXF descriptors are incomplete. AMA-linked clips don't support the same relink, multicam, or render behavior as imported/transcoded media. AAF sequences from another system don't relink because source timecode, tape, reel, or clip names differ. One specific trap is creating “Avid MXF” with a generic encoder and assuming Avid will treat it like media it created itself. FFmpeg can create many MXF files, and it can be very useful, but Avid OP-Atom compatibility has historically depended on metadata descriptors that generic muxers may not write exactly as Avid expects. Missing sampled width, sampled height, stored dimensions, or other CDCI descriptor fields can be enough to make otherwise valid media fail in Media Composer. For Avid-bound media, the safest approach is usually: Use Avid, Resolve, or another post-aware tool to generate Avid-compatible DNxHD/DNxHR MXF when the file must become managed Avid media. Use AAF plus linked camera originals when the conform needs to preserve source metadata. Avoid hand-dropping externally generated MXFs into Avid MediaFiles unless your team has tested that workflow with the same codec, frame rate, raster, and Media Composer version. Keep source timecode, clip name, and reel or tape metadata stable from dailies through conform. If the receiving editor says “Avid won’t take the MXF,” ask whether they mean it won't link, won't import, won't scan the media database, won't relink, or won't play correctly because those are different failures. Premiere-specific failure patterns Premiere Pro tends to accept a wide range of MXF files, but interoperability problems often appear later during audio prep, relink, proxy reconnect, or export. The most common Premiere MXF issue in mixed Avid workflows is audio channel interpretation. A file that appears as one 8-channel clip in Avid may appear as multiple mono clips or separate audio items in Premiere, and that can be normal based on how the MXF stores audio and how Premiere interprets the streams. Look at the FFprobe audio report before changing the project: ffprobe -hide_banner -v error \ -select_streams a \ -show_entries stream=index,codec_name,channels,channel_layout,sample_rate \ -of compact \ input.mxf If FFprobe shows one audio stream with eight channels, the issue is likely interpretation or track mapping. If it shows eight separate one-channel streams, the file is structurally different from a single interleaved multichannel stream. Both can be valid, but they aren't the same handoff. The same audio can be interpreted as one multichannel stream or several separate tracks. Premiere relink issues usually come from changed paths, moved media, renamed files, or proxies not matching the full-resolution media. Adobe’s own relink and proxy reconnect guidance focuses on reconnecting clips through the Link Media and full-resolution reconnect workflows. In practice, the metadata that matters most is: file name and path, for simple relink; media start timecode, for conform; duration, frame rate, and audio channel count; proxy and full-resolution relationships; reel, tape, or camera roll metadata when moving through AAF/XML. If you plan to grade, composite, mix, or finish outside Premiere, reconnect full-resolution media before export and inspect the interchange file in the destination app. Don't assume that a timeline that plays correctly in Premiere will automatically round-trip through AAF or XML with every track assignment, timecode value, and audio mapping intact. Resolve-specific failure patterns Resolve is commonly used as the bridge between Avid and finishing because it supports Avid DNxHD/DNxHR workflows and can exchange sequences using AAF. Avid’s own guidance describes two broad Media Composer to Resolve approaches : sending an AAF that links to original AMA-linked sources, or sending an AAF with rendered MXF media. Resolve can also render DNxHD or DNxHR MXF media back for Media Composer. That doesn't mean every MXF is safe because Resolve support depends on exact codec details. The supported formats list changes across versions, and some formats decode but don't encode, while others are limited by operating system or licensing. Resolve problems usually fall into a few buckets: The file is a camera MXF variant that the installed Resolve version doesn't decode. The file decodes, but metadata needed for conform is missing or mapped differently. Proxy generation fails for a specific camera codec or MXF flavor. AAF import succeeds, but clips link to the wrong media because reel or source timecode conflicts. Avid return media renders correctly, but Media Composer doesn't relink because the expected naming or tape metadata is different. For Avid and Resolve round trips, preserve the conform identifiers. Camera manufacturers and post workflow docs often emphasize the same thing: proxies and originals need matching source timecode and clip name or reel name. If those drift, the online conform becomes manual very quickly. A practical test matrix for mixed NLE workflows When a production has to move MXF media through Avid, Premiere, and Resolve, build a small test set before committing the whole show. Use real files from the camera, sound workflow, dailies process, and finishing path, and don't test with a generic sample clip. A useful test set includes: one normal camera clip; one long take; one high frame rate or off-speed clip; one clip with all expected audio channels; one clip with synced production sound; one proxy and its matching full-resolution source; one rendered DNxHD or DNxHR handoff file; one final delivery-style MXF with the required channel layout . Run each file through the actual operations the show will use: link, import, transcode, proxy, relink, AAF export, XML export, Resolve conform, Avid return, Premiere relink, and final export. Find the exact step where metadata or interpretation changes. Document the results in plain language: Avid 2024.x links XAVC-I OP1a via source browser, but your team must transcode to DNxHR LB for shared editorial. Premiere imports the same file, but audio appears as eight mono tracks. Resolve 20 reads the source and conforms from AAF when Resolve sources reel name from filename. Avid return from Resolve works when rendered as DNxHR HQX MXF using Avid-compatible settings. FFmpeg rewrap opens in Premiere and Resolve but Media Composer doesn't accept it as managed Avid media. That kind of note is more useful than “MXF compatible” because it describes the workflow, not just the extension. Rewrapping when the essence is fine Rewrapping means copying the video and audio essence into a new container without re-encoding, and it's fast and avoids generational quality loss. It can help when the receiving tool dislikes the container but supports the codec. Rewrapping changes the container while keeping the video and audio essence intact. For example, if a system accepts the codec in MOV better than MXF, a copy rewrap may be enough: ffmpeg -i input.mxf -map 0 -c copy output.mov For some OP1a MXF cases, remuxing to a fresh MXF may clean up simple container issues: ffmpeg -i input.mxf -map 0 -c copy output_rewrap.mxf But rewrapping won't fix unsupported codecs, bad timecode decisions, wrong audio mapping, or missing metadata that the destination requires. It also may not create Avid-native OP-Atom media that Media Composer will treat like its own database-managed files. After a rewrap, compare the original and output: ffprobe -hide_banner -v error -show_format -show_streams -print_format json input.mxf > original.json ffprobe -hide_banner -v error -show_format -show_streams -print_format json output_rewrap.mxf > rewrap.json Then test the rewrapped file in the actual destination application. If the problem was wrapper tolerance, you may be done. If the problem follows the file, the issue is probably codec, audio layout, or metadata. Re-encoding as the controlled last resort Re-encoding is the right move when the codec is unsupported, too heavy for the workflow, damaged, or inconsistent across systems. It's also common when standardizing edit media so all collaborators work with the same codec and raster. Good mezzanine choices depend on the facility and destination, but in Avid and Resolve workflows DNxHD and DNxHR are common because both applications support them well. Premiere also handles DNx media in professional workflows. A basic DNxHR transcode might look like this: ffmpeg -i input.mxf \ -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a? \ -c:v dnxhd -profile:v dnxhr_hq \ -c:a pcm_s24le \ output_dnxhr.mov That example is intentionally generic because real jobs need exact settings for frame rate, raster, field order, color range, channel count, and delivery requirements. For Avid-managed media, your team usually reduces risk by generating the files through Resolve, Media Composer, or a dailies system instead of relying on a generic encoder to produce drop-in Avid MXF. When re-encoding for editorial or finishing, protect the conform metadata: keep source timecode; keep source clip names; preserve reel, tape, or camera roll values where the workflow uses them; avoid changing frame rates unless that's an intentional edit decision; keep audio channel order documented; store the FFprobe report with the transcode batch. Transcoding is a workflow decision, and it only becomes dangerous when your team does it silently, with changed timecode, flattened audio, or undocumented naming. The clean decision path When an MXF breaks across Avid, Premiere, or Resolve, resist the urge to “just make a new file.” First inspect it, then decide which layer is failing. Use FFprobe to identify the wrapper, codec, stream layout, timecode, and metadata. Test the file in the exact app versions the team uses. Separate import problems from relink problems. Treat Avid linked media and Avid managed media as different workflows. Treat Premiere audio interpretation as something to inspect, not guess. Treat Resolve support as version-specific. Then choose the least destructive fix: reinterpret or remap audio when the streams are valid but presented incorrectly; relink using stable file names, timecode, reel, and clip metadata when the media is valid but offline; rewrap when the codec is supported and only the container is the problem; re-encode when the codec, performance profile, or application support makes it necessary. MXF interoperability is manageable when you stop treating .mxf as the answer. The extension is only the wrapper label, and the workflow depends on what is inside, how it was made, and what the next system needs to trust it. FAQ Rewrapping can help when the codec is supported but the receiving application dislikes the container structure. It copies the existing audio and video essence into a new wrapper without re-encoding, so it's fast and avoids quality loss. It won't fix an unsupported codec, incorrect audio mapping, missing conform metadata, or media that needs to become true Avid-managed OP-Atom media. FFprobe shows the actual contents of the MXF, including codec, profile, frame size, frame rate, pixel format, field order, stream count, audio channels, timecode, and metadata tags. This helps separate wrapper problems from codec problems and reveals whether audio is stored as one multichannel stream or multiple mono streams. MXF files can store audio in different ways, such as one interleaved multichannel stream or several mono streams. Each application may interpret those streams differently. If picture plays but audio is missing, split unexpectedly, or mapped to the wrong tracks, inspect the audio streams with FFprobe and then adjust channel interpretation or track mapping in the destination application. Source timecode, clip name, reel name, tape name, camera roll, file name, duration, frame rate, and audio channel count are commonly important. The exact fields depend on the workflow and application. If those values change during transcoding, proxy creation, or rewrapping, AAF, XML, and relink workflows can fail even when the media itself plays correctly. Re-encode when the receiving system can't decode the codec, the media is too heavy for the workflow, the file is damaged, or the production needs standardized editorial media. In Avid and Resolve workflows, DNxHD and DNxHR are common mezzanine choices. Re-encoding should preserve timecode, clip names, reel or tape metadata, frame rate, and documented audio channel order whenever those values are needed for conform. Multiple local copies can create false results because one assistant may be testing the original while another tests a rewrap or transcode. Aspect lets the team mount the same project media as one shared cloud filespace, so Avid, Premiere, and Resolve tests happen against the same file set.

title: Zipalertinib Plus Chemotherapy First-Line Phase 3 REZILIENT3 Trial Data Selected for Presidential Symposium Presentation at the IASLC 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer
summary: Presentation will feature results from the planned interim analysis of the Phase 3 REZILIENT3 trial, which met its primary endpoint of progression-free survival in first line EGFR exon 20 insertion mutation NSCLC PRINCETON, N.J., CAMBRIDGE, Mass., August 19, 2026 — Taiho Oncology, Inc.
body_text: Presentation will feature results from the planned interim analysis of the Phase 3 REZILIENT3 trial, which met its primary endpoint of progression-free survival in first line EGFR exon 20 insertion mutation NSCLC PRINCETON, N.J., CAMBRIDGE, Mass., August 19, 2026 — Taiho Oncology, Inc. and Cullinan Therapeutics, Inc. (Nasdaq: CGEM) today announced that results from the planned interim analysis of the Phase 3 REZILIENT3 trial have been selected for presentation in the Presidential Symposium 2 at the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer's (IASLC) 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC), to be held September 12-15, 2026, in Seoul, South Korea. REZILIENT3 evaluates zipalertinib plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone in the first-line treatment of patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) exon 20 insertion mutation-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The Presidential Symposium 2 is a premier plenary session featuring notable advances in lung cancer research and treatment with the potential to change clinical practice. Session information for the abstract is listed below. Full abstract details will be available via the conference website in accordance with IASLC embargo policies. Title: Zipalertinib plus Chemotherapy for 1st-line NSCLC with EGFR Exon 20 Insertions: Results from the Phase 3 Trial (REZILIENT3) Presenting Author: Dr. Daniel Tan Shao Weng, Duke Health, Singapore Session Name: PL03 Presidential Symposium 2 Including Lectureship Award Presentations Session Type: Presidential Symposium Session Date: Monday, September 14, 2026 Session Time: 8 a.m. KST Location: Plenary, Hall D2, 3F About the REZILIENT3 Trial This multicenter, randomized, controlled, open-label global trial enrolled 285 adults with previously untreated, locally advanced or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations. The primary objective of this trial is to assess progression-free survival in the zipalertinib plus chemotherapy arm versus the chemotherapy arm. About Zipalertinib Zipalertinib (development code: CLN-081/TAS6417) is an orally available small molecule designed to target activating mutations in EGFR. The molecule was selected because of its ability to inhibit EGFR variants with exon 20 insertion mutations. Zipalertinib is designed as a next generation, irreversible EGFR inhibitor for the treatment of a genetically defined subset of patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Zipalertinib is investigational and has not been approved by any health authority. Zipalertinib is being developed by Taiho Oncology, Inc., its parent company, Taiho Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., and in collaboration with Cullinan Therapeutics, Inc. in the U.S. About EGFR Exon 20 Insertion Mutations NSCLC is a common form of lung cancer and up to 4% of all cases globally have EGFR ex20ins.1 In the United States, approximately 16% of patients with NSCLC harbor EGFR mutations,1 with insertions at exon 20 accounting for up to 12% of these mutations.2 About Taiho Oncology, Inc. The mission of Taiho Oncology, Inc. is to improve the lives of patients with cancer, their families and their caregivers.
